title: Entering the room
hookLine: Balaam's words "how goodly are thy tents" are said on entering a synagogue

cards: Doorways change people. You lower your voice walking into a library. You straighten your back at a job interview.
At some homes you take your shoes off before anyone asks. A threshold is a small border.
In many synagogues, the first words people say on entering come from a surprising source: a foreign prophet who had been hired to curse.

teach.b: Back in Numbers, King Balak of Moab hires the prophet Balaam to curse Israel.
Balaam climbs a height, looks down at the camp spread across the valley, tribe by tribe, and blessing comes out of his mouth instead: "How goodly are thy tents, O Jacob, Thy dwellings, O Israel!"
In Hebrew, mah tovu: how good. What did he see? The Talmud, in Bava Batra, and Rashi after it, point to a detail.
The tents were set up so that no doorway faced another. Each family had its privacy: a huge camp, and no one peering into anyone else's home. The respect was visible from the hilltop.
The rabbis read tents and dwellings as houses of prayer and houses of study, so the verse became words for entering a synagogue.
In many siddurim, mah tovu stands at the very beginning of the morning prayers, followed by a psalm verse about coming into God's house through God's great kindness. And there's a twist.

teach.h: AN OUTSIDER'S WORDS AT THE DOOR.
teach.b: These are an outsider's words, someone sent to do harm, who looked closely and saw goodness.
A few later teachers were uneasy about opening prayer with Balaam's words. The custom stayed.
Some find it moving that, in many prayer books, the morning begins with what a stranger saw: a community that respects one another's doors.

how: Many Jews say mah tovu (Numbers 24:5) on entering a synagogue in the morning, followed by verses from the Psalms; in many siddurim it is the first passage of the morning service.

o: how good: words of blessing said on entering
how long: a cry of waiting in a hard time
who is like you: a song of praise at the sea

games.q: at the door — tap the pairs.
p: read as houses of prayer and study

s: mah tovu was first spoken by Moses
by Balaam, the foreign prophet hired to curse.
Rashi says the tents' doorways didn't face each other
following the Talmud in Bava Batra.

games.q: you're Balaam, paid by a king to curse the camp below. you look down at the tents and open your mouth. what comes out?
o: how goodly are thy tents, O Jacob.
games.why: a blessing, and centuries later the words people say at the synagogue door.

practice: Picture the next doorway you'll walk through, a home, a classroom, an office, a place of worship, and see yourself stopping just before it for a single breath. If you pray, mah tovu is there: how goodly are thy tents, O Jacob.
If not, notice what's good about the place you're about to enter, and the people inside.

wordCard.voice: Mah tovu. How good — Balaam's blessing on seeing Israel's tents, each respecting the other's doorway, said now on entering a synagogue.

orig.note: Hebrew: how good. Numbers 24:5, said on entering a synagogue.

carryVoice: Your line: how good these tents. A stranger came to curse, looked closely, and saw goodness. That's day five hundred forty-one.

sources.q: How goodly are thy tents, O Jacob, Thy dwellings, O Israel!
